selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: Contest-Aware Metahumor
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the entry comments on contests, media, or the act of submitting humor while remaining a functioning joke; score 0 when it is a generic statement unrelated to that machinery.
selected.rationale: R13, R21, and R51 derive extra force from recognizable contest or slogan conventions rather than operating as context-free jokes.
member_names: Delivers without explaining or winking at itself
Dependence on the contest prompt to become legible

selected.name: Economy: comedic payoff per word
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 the ratio of comedic payoff to text length: how much of the joke's full effect is delivered in very few words versus requiring a long wind-up to reach a comparably small payoff. 10 = maximal payoff landed in a handful of words. 0 = long entry required to arrive at a comparably small or absent payoff.
selected.rationale: R07 ('I'M WITH STUPID', three words, full payoff) and R60 ('U.N. Resolution', two words) both land completely in minimal text and score dense_high/card_low, contrasted with the much longer paragraph-length R13 which delivers a comparatively soft single joke.

selected.name: Reference With Comic Function
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural or personal reference actively creates the joke’s tension or reversal; score 0 when the reference is merely decorative or obscure without comic work.
selected.rationale: The figures in R16, R33, and R55 supply the central contrast, while the long proper name in R08 can stand without generating an additional idea.

selected.name: Logical Collapse Depth
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a statement initially sounds sensible but fails under a specific second reading; score 0 when it is a truism, tautology, or merely grammatical statement.
selected.rationale: R12 and R38 invite assent before undermining their own logic, whereas R37 mainly reverses familiar words without a comparable collapse.

selected.name: Vivid Comic Scene
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the wording creates a specific, easily pictured situation that carries the humor; score 0 when it remains an abstract label or unelaborated assertion.
selected.rationale: R09 supplies the striking image of all-you-can-eat communion, while R20 supplies concrete medical, insurance, and social details that make its premise vivid.

selected.name: Readable Contradiction
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an apparent contradiction follows from a precise, instantly understandable clash of meanings; score 0 when it is merely short, technically paradoxical, or semantically arbitrary.
selected.rationale: R17’s “Low-Speed Chase” presents a clean semantic collision, while R54’s “Yom Kippur” offers much less evident contradiction from the text alone.

selected.name: Self-demonstrating execution (the entry enacts its own claim)
selected.instruction: Score whether the entry performs the property it is talking about, so that its form and its content collide. 10 = the text is an instance of the very thing it names or denies, and the collision is the joke (e.g. a word that violates its own definition, a statement whose confident structure is exactly what makes its content vacuous). 5 = form and content are consistent but the form adds a small extra layer. 0 = form is a neutral container for the content. Score the collision, not general cleverness.
selected.rationale: R34 ('Monosyllabic' as an oxymoron) is a five-syllable word meaning one-syllable; R26 and R44 are Yogi-isms whose grammar is impeccably assertive while the proposition is either a tautology or self-cancelling. All three are dense-high/card-low. A criterion bank built around topic, cleverness and clarity will not see that the sentence is doing something to itself; it will just see a short quoted sentence.
member_names: Self-demonstrating execution (the entry enacts its own claim)

selected.name: Multi-layered simultaneous wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how many distinct, independent meanings or resonances the entry's central wordplay activates at once. 10 = the pun/phrase works on two or more genuinely separate semantic layers simultaneously (e.g. it is literally true of the referenced person's public reputation AND fits the contest's formal template AND carries a secondary double meaning). 0 = a single flat, one-layer substitution with no secondary resonance beyond the obvious swap.
selected.rationale: R16 ('anticlimactically' for Pee-wee Herman) and R38 ('disappointedly' for Zoe Baird, punning on dis-appointed/withdrawn-nomination) both stack a generic Tom Swifty adverb-match with a second layer tied to the person's real situation, while R08 ('Golden Reliever') is a flat single-layer swap; this layering gap plausibly explains why dense ranks the former much higher than the scorecard does.

selected.name: Topical/biographical knowledge required to resolve joke
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's comedic payoff depends on the reader already knowing a specific real-world scandal, event, or fact tied to a named person or institution, versus being resolvable purely from the words on the page. 10 = the entry is inert or meaningless without that outside knowledge. 0 = fully self-contained; no external knowledge of any specific event is needed.
selected.rationale: R11 ('Dr. Cecil Jacobson for Jiffy Pop Popcorn') only lands if the reader knows Jacobson's fertility-fraud scandal, and R56 ('Richie Petitbon said absently') only lands if the reader knows Petitbon's disastrous playoff coaching record; both score high dense/low card, unlike self-contained R33 (chiasmus).
member_names: Topical/biographical knowledge required to resolve joke

selected.name: Crude/taboo content as sole comedic engine
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's laugh depends on scatological, sexual, or taboo subject matter carrying the joke essentially by itself, with little additional wit layered on top. 10 = shock/crude content alone is doing nearly all the work. 0 = no reliance on taboo content; humor (if any) comes from elsewhere.
selected.rationale: R23 ('The Heimlich Manure') and R36 ('1, 2, breasts . . .') both lean on scatological/sexual content for the whole joke and both are dense_low/card_high, suggesting the scorecard may over-credit crude one-trick puns that the dense model discounts as unsophisticated.
member_names: Crude/taboo content as sole comedic engine

selected.name: Cliché Reassignment
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar slogan, quotation, or title is relocated so its usual implication becomes newly comic; score 0 when the familiar phrase remains unchanged or is attached arbitrarily.
selected.rationale: R03 and R29 repurpose recognizable slogans through their contest context, while R40 relies more directly on a familiar song title without a comparable reassignment.

selected.name: Formal-structure discipline (meter/rhyme/reversal precision)
selected.instruction: For entries constrained by a named literary form (limerick, chiasmus, Tom Swifty, haiku, etc.), score 0-10 how precisely and cleanly the entry satisfies that form's meter, rhyme scheme, grammatical reversal, or other structural constraint. 10 = the form is executed with no metrical, rhyme, or structural flaws. 0 = the form is badly broken, ignored, or barely attempted.
selected.rationale: R19 (the chiasmus 'Being nice isn't easy, and being easy isn't nice' executes a clean AB/BA reversal) and R42 (the limerick keeps clean AABBA rhyme and meter across all five lines) both score dense_low/card_high, testing whether mechanical form-compliance alone is driving the scorecard's high ratings independent of actual wit.

selected.name: Found phrase reframed rather than invented
selected.instruction: Score whether the entry takes an existing, unaltered phrase from the world and makes it funny purely by placing it in the contest's frame. 10 = the phrase is quoted exactly as it exists in ordinary use, and the entire comic work is done by the new frame, which reveals a property the phrase always had but nobody had named. 5 = an existing phrase is used but with modification or added scaffolding. 0 = the entry manufactures a novel string that has no life outside this entry. Note that this criterion can be high while surface effort looks near zero.
selected.rationale: Several dense-high/card-low rows are unmodified found phrases whose only intervention is the frame: R03 ('Yom Kippur' offered as an oxymoron), R06 ('I'M WITH STUPID' on a self-mocking contest T-shirt), R30 ('U.N. Resolution'), R43 ('Low-Speed Chase'), R55 ('Chuck 3:16'). To a scorecard these look like the lowest-effort submissions in the pool - no construction, no elaboration - which plausibly drives their low card percentiles despite dense percentiles of 0.79 to 0.95.
member_names: Found phrase reframed rather than invented

selected.name: Mutual Semantic Lock
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the entry’s parts make one another newly meaningful or surprising; score 0 when its parts merely coexist without a reciprocal connection.
selected.rationale: The quoted statements and adverbs in R14, R20, and R31 create linked meanings, unlike the loosely assembled components in R28.

selected.name: Perspective Reversal
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the entry makes a familiar institution, relationship, or activity absurd by shifting the reader’s viewpoint; score 0 when it merely describes an odd object or situation.
selected.rationale: R34 reframes communion through buffet language, R35 reframes presidential propriety, and R55 turns endorsement itself into the comic target.

selected.name: In-group reference to the column and its rituals
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text refers to the contest itself, its running jokes, its recurring apparatus, or the experience of entering it, as opposed to referring only to the world outside. 10 = the column, its prizes, its rituals, its regulars or its self-mocking house identity are the explicit subject of the text. 5 = a passing venue-insider allusion or a coinage that only parses to someone who reads the column regularly. 0 = no reference to the contest or its community anywhere in the text. Score presence and prominence of the in-group reference only. You must NOT judge whether the self-reference is charming, tiresome, or well-executed, and must not treat insider fluency as evidence of quality.
selected.rationale: In-group reference lands on both sides of the disagreement and so is predictive without being about the entry's merit: R54 ('Entering the Style Invitational: I used to enter Publishers Clearing House sweepstakes...') and R53 ('I love you more than The Style Invitational') are card-high, while R43 ('Chuck 3:16') and R55 ('I'M WITH STUPID', both from the contest's own T-shirt prompt) are dense-high, and R08 ('Pub-it: n. A unit of measure...') coins a house term. The upstream factor - community tenure - plausibly also improves real entries, hence mixed=true.
member_names: In-group reference to the column and its rituals
selected.upstream_parent: the submitter's embeddedness in the column's readership community (how long and how closely they have followed it)
upstream_parent_all_members: the submitter's embeddedness in the column's readership community (how long and how closely they have followed it)

selected.name: Byline metadata residue
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the visible text includes appended author names, locations, or single-author parenthetical credits rather than entry content. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the credited author or entry is good.
selected.rationale: Names and locations can act as proxies for reputation, familiarity, or local identity, while practiced authors may also write better entries. Examples include R04, R07, and R51.
upstream_parent_all_members: author reputation, following, or established entrant status

selected.name: Proper-name density
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how densely the entry contains named people, places, institutions, brands, songs, or titles; count visible entities only and do not judge their appropriateness.
selected.rationale: R10 contains Richie Petitbon and playoff games, while R37 combines Dr. Cecil Jacobson with Jiffy Pop; R49 adds two names and a song title. Entity density is a topical and lexical signal, not itself a quality attribute.
upstream_parent_all_members: the contest prompt's own explicit formal requirement in several prompts to include 'a reference to a famous person or institution' (a structural, prompt-driven feature rather than a discretionary authorial quality choice)

selected.name: Dated cultural anchoring
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry depends on period-bound people, technologies, institutions, or media, such as obsolete devices or strongly era-specific references. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the references are good or funny.
selected.rationale: Temporal familiarity and nostalgia can affect how text is processed independently of its construction as an entry. Examples include R05, R51, and R60.
upstream_parent_all_members: submission timing or period-specific cultural familiarity

selected.name: Coauthor signature
selected.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text visibly signals multiple authors, joint credit, or collaborative production; do not judge whether collaboration improves the entry.
selected.rationale: R24 credits two contributors and R49 credits Michelle and Warren Uhler. Collaboration can alter how a submission is treated and can also affect the actual construction of the text, so this channel is mixed.

selected.name: Joint-byline and recurring-name fingerprint in the credit
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW STRONGLY the visible credit apparatus signals a practised or collaborating submitter rather than a one-off individual. 10 = two or more named submitters sharing one entry, a household pair, or a semicolon-joined multi-person credit. 5 = a single named submitter whose name or locality is formatted with unusual completeness (middle initial, out-of-state qualifier, formal styling). 0 = a plain single name, or no credit at all. Score only what the credit string looks like. You must NOT judge whether collaboration or practice is good, must not speculate about the person's skill, and must not let this affect any read on the entry's humour.
selected.rationale: The slice contains several joint credits - R29 ('Sandra Hull, Arlington, and Stu Solomon, Springfield'), R44 ('Paul Styrene, Olney; Elden Carnahan, Laurel'), R42 ('Michelle and Warren Uhler'), R52 ('Andrea and Alan Pendleton') - and visible name recurrence across items, with 'Paul Kondis, Alexandria' credited on both R40 and R41 and a Sorensen of Herndon on both R20 and R35. A practised entrant is plausibly upstream of both the credit-string shape and, honestly, of writing better entries, so this is tagged mixed; but the fingerprint itself is a byline formatting feature and must never be creditable in the bank.
member_names: Joint-byline and recurring-name fingerprint in the credit
selected.upstream_parent: the submitter's practice and social organisation in this format (habitual entrants, entrant pairs, entrant circles)
upstream_parent_all_members: crowding of the entry-pool container (multiple independent entrants submitted the same or a near-identical idea, so the editor credited more than one of them together -- a fingerprint of how common/obvious that specific idea was among the whole submission stream)
the submitter's practice and social organisation in this format (habitual entrants, entrant pairs, entrant circles)

selected.name: Raw length, clause count and syntactic elaboration
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW LONG and syntactically elaborated the text is, in absolute terms. 10 = multiple sentences or many subordinate clauses, roughly 30 words or more, with embedded qualifications. 5 = one full sentence of ordinary length. 0 = a bare phrase of one to three words. Count words and clauses; ignore verse line breaks and count the running text. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate to the format, whether the text is padded or economical, or whether brevity is a virtue here. This is a raw size measurement.
selected.rationale: Among the prose items, the two longest strings in the slice are both card-high - R54 (a three-clause anecdote) and R32 (a heavily front-loaded question about estimating a basketball player's height) - while the shortest strings are dense-high, R41 ('Monosyllabic', one word) and R55 ('I'M WITH STUPID'). Raw size is trivially readable by any model and correlates with per-criterion elaboration credit. Tagged mixed because economy is arguably a real virtue in this format, so the discounted and undiscounted readouts should both be reported.
member_names: Raw length, clause count and syntactic elaboration

selected.name: Morphological wordplay
selected.instruction: Rate from 0 (absent) to 10 (pervasive) how much the entry uses spelling changes, homophones, portmanteaus, or near-word substitutions. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the wordplay is good, funny, or effective.
selected.rationale: A text system may latch onto conspicuous lexical mutations as an easy humor proxy, although their presence does not establish entry quality. Examples include R27, R36, and R45.

selected.name: Interrogative/question-form surface syntax
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's surface syntax takes question form (begins with an interrogative word such as 'What,' 'Who,' 'Why,' or 'How,' and/or ends with a question mark). 0 = entry is not phrased as a question at all; 10 = entry is fully phrased as a direct question in both opening word and terminal punctuation. Score only this surface syntactic feature; do not judge whether the question itself is clever.
selected.rationale: R21 ('What is the opposite of a head count?') and R37 ('Who wrote "Profiles in Scourge"?') both take full interrogative surface form as required by their Jeopardy-style prompt, unlike declarative entries such as R18 ('USS Powderkeg'); this syntactic marker is largely a prompt-genre template effect rather than a signal of the entry's own comedic quality.
selected.upstream_parent: surface-only (a template feature largely forced by the 'Jeopardy!' prompt's own answer-to-question genre requirement, not an independent authorial quality choice)
upstream_parent_all_members: surface-only (a template feature largely forced by the 'Jeopardy!' prompt's own answer-to-question genre requirement, not an independent authorial quality choice)

selected.name: Segmentation artifact: truncation and container-label prefixes
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text shows signs of having been cut out of a larger record rather than standing as a whole submission. 10 = the text is unmistakably a fragment: it breaks off mid-sentence or mid-phrase, ends in a bare dash or colon with nothing after it, or consists only of an item label carried over from the surrounding layout (e.g. a parenthetical figure label or a numbered quote header) with no body. 5 = the text is grammatically complete but opens with a carried-over label, prefix or numbering that is clearly part of the container's layout rather than of the entry. 0 = a clean, self-contained string with no layout residue and no truncation. Score the mechanical evidence of cutting only. You must NOT judge whether a fragment is a bad entry, and must not infer merit or its absence from the fragment's content.
selected.rationale: Fragments occupy the extreme tail of the dense percentiles in this slice - R09 ('(Cartoon A) This is a beguiling', 0.999), R11 ('(Cartoon E) --', 0.998), R39 ('(Cartoon D) --', 0.997), R50 ('Quote 1: You will rejoice to hear...', 0.975) - while a different family of fragments sits at the top of the card percentiles, e.g. R46 ('Something That Will Never Become an Olympic Sport --') and R15 ('A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It:'). Both extremes are being driven by how the row was cut, not by any property of an entry, which makes this the clearest declared nuisance in the slice.
member_names: Segmentation artifact: truncation and container-label prefixes
selected.upstream_parent: record segmentation - how the printed column was split into individual item rows during corpus construction
